formats.craft: A craft story. Maker, material, process — as far as the country file goes, and no further.
formats.culture: A culture story. What is kept and who keeps it, named as particular communities rather than as a continent.
formats.essay: A photo essay. Between five and twelve frames, each with its own caption, no image dumping.
formats.food: A food story. Ingredient-to-table order, wide plates.
formats.heritage: A heritage story. Dated where the dataset holds a date, undated where it does not, and never invented either way.
formats.journey: A journey story. Built from the geography file, not from prose: where a country actually borders, and what is on the other side.
formats.note: A short note. One or two write-ups, set large, no furniture.
formats.now: A contemporary panel. Cities, building, business, what is being made this decade.
formats.people: A people story. Portrait proportions, the write-ups stacked, a Local Voice slot that stays empty until somebody real has been asked.
formats.wild: A field guide. What is here, when, and what is being done to keep it.

stories.arcTitle: The first thing you would see
stories.asks: What does this country open with?
stories.text: Two and a half million people, a hundred and thirty thousand elephant, and space for both.
stories.title: Fewer People Than Elephants

stories.asks: Who lives here, and who is speaking?
stories.text: Tracking with San guides, who will find in an hour what nobody else sees at all.
stories.title: The Kalahari San

stories.asks: What is eaten here?
stories.text: Slow-pounded beef and sorghum porridge, and braai wherever there is a fire.
stories.title: Seswaa and Bogobe

stories.asks: What is made here, and who makes it?
stories.text: Palm baskets woven in the delta panhandle, dyed with bark, and collected worldwide.
stories.title: Basketry

stories.asks: What is kept, and who keeps it?
stories.text: Setswana across the country, and San communities in the Kalahari with the oldest culture on earth.
stories.title: Batswana and San

stories.asks: What happened here, and what is left of it?
stories.text: Independent since 1966, and the one African country that used its diamonds well.
stories.title: Diamonds and Democracy

stories.asks: What is it like to live here this decade?
stories.text: Not really cities — two safari towns with airstrips, which is what the country needs.
stories.title: Maun and Kasane

stories.arcTitle: What is wild, and what is being kept wild
stories.asks: What lives here, and who is protecting it?
stories.text: Chobe holds more elephant than anywhere on earth, and they come to the river at four.
stories.title: The Largest Elephant Population

stories.asks: What is the shape of this country?
stories.text: Water in the north, salt pans in the middle, and Kalahari sand for the rest of it.
stories.title: Delta, Pan and Desert

stories.asks: What would you not have found on your own?
stories.text: Drive onto the pan at night and there is no horizon and no sound at all.
stories.title: The Makgadikgadi

stories.arcTitle: The first thing you would see
stories.asks: What does this country open with?
stories.text: Sea level to Sahel in nine hundred kilometres, French and English on the same road, and almost nobody else on it.
stories.title: Everything, Within One Border

stories.asks: Who lives here, and who is speaking?
stories.text: Two hundred and fifty ethnic groups and as many languages, from the Mafa terraces of the Mandara to the Fulani of the Sahel.
stories.title: Fulani, Mafa and Bamileke

stories.asks: What is eaten here?
stories.text: Bitterleaf and groundnut ndolé, plantain, and whole fish grilled on the sand at Kribi within sight of the boat.
stories.title: Ndole, Poulet DG and Grilled Fish

stories.asks: What is made here, and who makes it?
stories.text: Lost-wax bronze, beaded thrones and carved masks made on the craft street the same way they were three centuries ago.
stories.title: The Foumban Bronze Casters

stories.asks: What is kept, and who keeps it?
stories.text: Bamileke and Bamoun chiefdoms in the west, still functioning, with palaces, secret societies and their own calendars.
stories.title: The Grassfields Kingdoms

stories.asks: What happened here, and what is left of it?
stories.text: The Dja Faunal Reserve is UNESCO World Heritage; the volcanic spires above Rhumsiki are the image on the old banknote.
stories.title: Dja, Rhumsiki and the Mandara

stories.asks: What is it like to live here this decade?
stories.text: The port that moves the country and the hill capital that governs it, ninety minutes apart by air and nothing alike.
stories.title: Douala and Yaounde

stories.arcTitle: What is wild, and what is being kept wild
stories.asks: What lives here, and who is protecting it?
stories.text: Forest elephants, drills and chimpanzees in Korup and Dja — one of the oldest and least disturbed rainforests in Africa.
stories.title: Wildlife of the Rainforest

stories.asks: What is the shape of this country?
stories.text: The Cameroon Volcanic Line runs from the Gulf of Guinea to the Mandara mountains, changing the landscape every two hours of driving.
stories.title: Six Climates, One Country

stories.asks: What would you not have found on your own?
stories.text: Black lava tongues from the 1999 and 2000 flows running down to the sea near Bakingili, with green already coming back.
stories.title: The 1999 Lava Fields

stories.arcTitle: The first thing you would see
stories.asks: What does this country open with?
stories.text: The largest economy in francophone West Africa, and the easiest of them to travel.
stories.title: The Engine of the Region

stories.asks: Who lives here, and who is speaking?
stories.text: Baoulé weaving, Senufo sculpture, and Dan masks from the western hills.
stories.title: Baoulé, Senufo and Dan

stories.asks: What is eaten here?
stories.text: Attiéké with grilled fish, and kedjenou slow-cooked in a sealed pot.
stories.title: Attiéké and Kedjenou

stories.asks: What is made here, and who makes it?
stories.text: Baoulé strip cloth, Korhogo painted cloth, and Dan masks carved for use rather than sale.
stories.title: Weaving and Carving

stories.asks: What is kept, and who keeps it?
stories.text: Akan, Krou, Mandé and Gur — around sixty peoples inside one border.
stories.title: Sixty Peoples

stories.asks: What happened here, and what is left of it?
stories.text: A basilica larger than Saint Peter's, built in the founder's home village.
stories.title: Yamoussoukro

stories.asks: What is it like to live here this decade?
stories.text: The Plateau's towers, the Ébrié lagoon, and a nightlife the region measures itself against.
stories.title: Abidjan

stories.arcTitle: What is wild, and what is being kept wild
stories.asks: What lives here, and who is protecting it?
stories.text: Pygmy hippo and chimpanzees at Taï, and Comoé's savanna in the north-east.
stories.title: Taï and Comoé

stories.asks: What is the shape of this country?
stories.text: Rainforest in the south-west, a lagoon coast, and savanna running north to Mali.
stories.title: Forest to Savanna

stories.asks: What would you not have found on your own?
stories.text: The western hills, with waterfalls, mask villages and a mountain nobody climbs.
stories.title: Man

stories.arcTitle: The first thing you would see
stories.asks: What does this country open with?
stories.text: People have been travelling to see this country for two and a half thousand years.
stories.title: The Oldest Journey

stories.asks: Who lives here, and who is speaking?
stories.text: Nubian villages above Aswan and Bedouin communities in the Sinai and the Western Desert.
stories.title: Nubians and Bedouin

stories.asks: What is eaten here?
stories.text: Breakfast is ful and bread; lunch is koshary; both are older than most cuisines.
stories.title: Ful, Koshary and Bread

stories.asks: What is made here, and who makes it?
stories.text: Hand-blown glass in Cairo, Egyptian cotton, and papyrus made the way it always was.
stories.title: Papyrus, Glass and Cotton

stories.asks: What is kept, and who keeps it?
stories.text: Three layers still in daily use, sometimes in the same street in old Cairo.
stories.title: Coptic, Islamic, Pharaonic

stories.asks: What happened here, and what is left of it?
stories.text: Karnak took two thousand years to build; Abu Simbel was moved sixty metres to save it.
stories.title: Karnak, Luxor, Abu Simbel

stories.asks: What is it like to live here this decade?
stories.text: Twenty million people on the Nile, and a Mediterranean city that remembers being Greek.
stories.title: Cairo and Alexandria

stories.arcTitle: What is wild, and what is being kept wild
stories.asks: What lives here, and who is protecting it?
stories.text: Two million migrating birds use the Delta and the Red Sea coast as a flyway each year.
stories.title: Birds of the Delta

stories.asks: What is the shape of this country?
stories.text: A green ribbon a few kilometres wide, and sand for a thousand kilometres either side of it.
stories.title: The Nile and the Desert

stories.asks: What would you not have found on your own?
stories.text: Eight hundred kilometres west, a Berber-speaking oasis with its own language and salt lakes.
stories.title: Siwa

stories.arcTitle: The first thing you would see
stories.asks: What does this country open with?
stories.text: No colonial period, its own script, its own calendar, and its own year that starts in September.
stories.title: Nothing Else Like It

stories.asks: Who lives here, and who is speaking?
stories.text: The lower Omo holds sixteen peoples in one valley, and the visits should be arranged carefully.
stories.title: Omo Valley

stories.asks: What is eaten here?
stories.text: Sourdough injera under everything, and fasting food that has made vegans of visitors.
stories.title: Injera and Doro Wat

stories.asks: What is made here, and who makes it?
stories.text: Handwoven shemma cotton, and Coptic crosses in silver, each region with its own shape.
stories.title: Weaving and Silver

stories.asks: What is kept, and who keeps it?
stories.text: Its own alphabet, its own calendar with thirteen months, and its own church since the fourth century.
stories.title: Its Own Everything

stories.asks: What happened here, and what is left of it?
stories.text: The Aksumite stelae, and the seventeenth-century castles of Gondar built by Fasilides.
stories.title: Aksum and Gondar

stories.asks: What is it like to live here this decade?
stories.text: Founded 1886, at 2,355 metres, and the diplomatic capital of the continent.
stories.title: Addis Ababa

stories.arcTitle: What is wild, and what is being kept wild
stories.asks: What lives here, and who is protecting it?
stories.text: The gelada lives nowhere else on earth, and grazes the Simien escarpment in troops of hundreds.
stories.title: Gelada and Walia Ibex

stories.asks: What is the shape of this country?
stories.text: The Rift Valley cuts the whole country in half, with highlands either side of it.
stories.title: Escarpment and Rift

stories.asks: What would you not have found on your own?
stories.text: Rock churches in cliff faces reached by hand and foot, with almost nobody else there.
stories.title: Tigray

stories.arcTitle: The first thing you would see
stories.asks: What does this country open with?
stories.text: English, good roads, a short flight from Europe, and everything within a day's drive.
stories.title: The Gentle Introduction

stories.asks: Who lives here, and who is speaking?
stories.text: Kente weaving in Volta and Ashanti, and the Dagbon drumming traditions of the north.
stories.title: The Ewe and the Dagomba

stories.asks: What is eaten here?
stories.text: The jollof argument is unwinnable; the tilapia off the grill with banku settles it.
stories.title: Jollof, Banku and Grilled Tilapia

stories.asks: What is made here, and who makes it?
stories.text: Kente woven in strips at Bonwire, and adinkra symbols stamped by hand at Ntonso.
stories.title: Kente and Adinkra

stories.asks: What is kept, and who keeps it?
stories.text: A kingdom that fought the British to a standstill, and still keeps its own court at Kumasi.
stories.title: Ashanti

stories.asks: What happened here, and what is left of it?
stories.text: Ghana asked the diaspora to come back, and a great many people did.
stories.title: The Year of Return

stories.asks: What is it like to live here this decade?
stories.text: Accra on the Atlantic, and Kumasi's Kejetia — one of the largest markets in West Africa.
stories.title: Accra and Kumasi

stories.arcTitle: What is wild, and what is being kept wild
stories.asks: What lives here, and who is protecting it?
stories.text: Elephants that walk into the camp waterhole at Mole, and forest elephants at Ankasa.
stories.title: Mole and Ankasa

stories.asks: What is the shape of this country?
stories.text: Rainforest and lagoon in the south, transitional woodland through the middle, savanna at Mole.
stories.title: Coast to Savanna

stories.asks: What would you not have found on your own?
stories.text: A village built entirely on stilts over Lake Tandane, reached only by canoe.
stories.title: Nzulezo

stories.arcTitle: The first thing you would see
stories.asks: What does this country open with?
stories.text: Migration, glacier, reef and desert inside one border, with the infrastructure to see all four in a fortnight.
stories.title: Magical Kenya

stories.asks: Who lives here, and who is speaking?
stories.text: Samburu in the northern drylands, Maasai in the south, both still moving cattle between seasonal grazing.
stories.title: Samburu and Maasai

stories.asks: What is eaten here?
stories.text: Goat roasted over charcoal, maize meal, sukuma wiki, and coastal biryani that came in by dhow.
stories.title: Nyama Choma and Ugali

stories.asks: What is made here, and who makes it?
stories.text: Maasai beadwork, Kisii soapstone carving, and kiondo sisal baskets made the way they always were.
stories.title: Beadwork and Kisii Stone

stories.asks: What is kept, and who keeps it?
stories.text: Two Kenyas: the cattle-keeping highlands and the coral-stone, Arabic-inflected coast.
stories.title: Maasai and Swahili

stories.asks: What happened here, and what is left of it?
stories.text: The oldest continuously inhabited Swahili settlement, carved doors, coral rag walls and no room for a car.
stories.title: Lamu Old Town

stories.asks: What is it like to live here this decade?
stories.text: The only capital on earth with a national park inside the city limits, and lions in sight of the skyline.
stories.title: Nairobi, Green City in the Sun

stories.arcTitle: What is wild, and what is being kept wild
stories.asks: What lives here, and who is protecting it?
stories.text: The Big Five, plus the reticulated giraffe and Grevy's zebra that live nowhere south of here.
stories.title: Wildlife on the Savannah

stories.asks: What is the shape of this country?
stories.text: The escarpment drops away below the Naivasha road, holding a chain of soda lakes and dormant volcanoes.
stories.title: The Great Rift Valley

stories.asks: What would you not have found on your own?
stories.text: The desert north: Chalbi's salt pan, Marsabit's forested crater and the road down to Lake Turkana.
stories.title: Chalbi and Marsabit

stories.arcTitle: The first thing you would see
stories.asks: What does this country open with?
stories.text: Lemurs, baobabs, tsingy, spiny forest — none of it exists anywhere else on earth.
stories.title: Nowhere Else

stories.asks: Who lives here, and who is speaking?
stories.text: The ancestors are present here in a way that shapes the calendar and the architecture.
stories.title: Famadihana and the Ancestors

stories.asks: What is eaten here?

stories.title: Romazava and Rice

stories.asks: What is made here, and who makes it?

stories.title: Silk, Raffia and Zafimaniry

stories.asks: What is kept, and who keeps it?

stories.title: Pirates and Kingdoms

stories.asks: What is it like to live here this decade?
stories.text: A capital built up twelve hills, with stairs instead of streets in half of it.
stories.title: Antananarivo

stories.arcTitle: What is wild, and what is being kept wild
stories.asks: What lives here, and who is protecting it?
stories.text: A hundred and seven species and subspecies of lemur, every one of them endemic.
stories.title: A Hundred Kinds of Lemur

stories.asks: What is the shape of this country?
stories.text: Rainforest east, highlands centre, spiny forest south, dry deciduous west, and reef all round.
stories.title: Six Ecosystems on One Island

stories.asks: What would you not have found on your own?
stories.text: The largest protected rainforest in the country, reached by boat, with whales in the bay.
stories.title: Masoala

stories.arcTitle: The first thing you would see
stories.asks: What does this country open with?
stories.text: A Hindu festival, a Creole kitchen, a French road name and a Chinese shop, in one street.
stories.title: Four Cultures, One Lagoon

stories.asks: Who lives here, and who is speaking?
stories.text: Creole spoken by everyone, Bhojpuri in the villages, and French and English in print.
stories.title: Creole and Bhojpuri

stories.asks: What is eaten here?
stories.text: Dholl puri off a street cart, rougaille at home, and a fish vindaye that is entirely local.
stories.title: Dholl Puri and Rougaille

stories.asks: What is made here, and who makes it?

stories.title: Model Ships and Textiles

stories.asks: What is kept, and who keeps it?
stories.text: Indian, African, French and Chinese, in one Creole language and one calendar.
stories.title: Four Continents

stories.asks: What happened here, and what is left of it?
stories.text: The mountain where escaped slaves lived at the top, and a world heritage site for that reason.
stories.title: Le Morne

stories.asks: What is it like to live here this decade?
stories.text: A working port and capital, with a market, a waterfront and the Champ de Mars.
stories.title: Port Louis

stories.arcTitle: What is wild, and what is being kept wild
stories.asks: What lives here, and who is protecting it?
stories.text: The dodo is gone, but the pink pigeon and the kestrel were both brought back from single figures.
stories.title: What the Dodo Left

stories.asks: What is the shape of this country?
stories.text: Lagoon all the way round, sugar cane across the plain, and gorges cut into the plateau.
stories.title: Lagoon and Gorge

stories.asks: What would you not have found on your own?
stories.text: Six hundred kilometres east, a tenth the size, and the island Mauritius used to be.
stories.title: Rodrigues

stories.arcTitle: The first thing you would see
stories.asks: What does this country open with?
stories.text: Surf in the morning, cedar forest by lunch, and the Sahara the following evening.
stories.title: Two Days, Four Climates

stories.text: Village life at two thousand metres, where the year is still organised around the snow.
stories.title: The People of the Atlas

stories.title: Tagine, Bread and Mint

stories.asks: What is kept, and who keeps it?
stories.text: Three Amazigh languages, Arabic, French and Spanish, and a culture that predates all of them.
stories.title: Amazigh and Arab

stories.asks: What happened here, and what is left of it?
stories.text: Fez, Marrakesh, Meknes and Rabat — four capitals, each of a different dynasty.
stories.title: The Imperial Cities

stories.asks: What is it like to live here this decade?
stories.text: Jemaa el-Fnaa at dusk, and the Atlantic modernism of Casablanca an hour up the road.
stories.title: Marrakesh and Casablanca

stories.arcTitle: What is wild, and what is being kept wild
stories.asks: What lives here, and who is protecting it?
stories.text: Macaques in the cedar forest above Azrou, and goats standing in the argan trees near Essaouira.
stories.title: Barbary Macaques and the Argan Forest

stories.asks: What is the shape of this country?
stories.text: Palm oases strung along the Draa, and gorges cut red through the Dades and the Todra.
stories.title: The Draa and the Dades

stories.asks: What would you not have found on your own?

stories.title: Chefchaouen and the Rif

stories.arcTitle: The first thing you would see
stories.asks: What does this country open with?
stories.text: Two thousand kilometres of Indian Ocean, and most of it still without a road to it.
stories.title: The Coast Nobody Has Ruined Yet

stories.asks: Who lives here, and who is speaking?

stories.title: Makonde and Makua

stories.asks: What is eaten here?

stories.title: Peri-Peri and Matapa

stories.asks: What is made here, and who makes it?
stories.text: Makonde blackwood carving, and the palm basketry of the northern islands.
stories.title: Carving and Basketry

stories.asks: What is kept, and who keeps it?
stories.text: Five hundred years of Portuguese on a Swahili coast, and a culture made from both.
stories.title: Portuguese and Swahili

stories.asks: What happened here, and what is left of it?
stories.text: Ibo, Angoche and Sofala — Indian Ocean trading towns older than the Portuguese.
stories.title: The Swahili Coast

stories.asks: What is it like to live here this decade?
stories.text: Wide avenues, a Mediterranean seafront, and the market Eiffel's company built.
stories.title: Maputo

stories.arcTitle: What is wild, and what is being kept wild
stories.asks: What lives here, and who is protecting it?
stories.text: A park that lost almost everything in the war and has spent twenty years getting it back.
stories.title: Gorongosa

stories.asks: What is the shape of this country?
stories.text: Coral reef the whole coast, miombo woodland inland, and the Rift's southern end at Gorongosa.
stories.title: Reef and Miombo

stories.asks: What would you not have found on your own?
stories.text: Silversmiths, a fort, mangrove channels, and about as far from a resort as it gets.
stories.title: Ibo Island

stories.arcTitle: The first thing you would see
stories.asks: What does this country open with?
stories.text: Two and a half million people in a country twice the size of Germany.
stories.title: Space, and the Silence in It

stories.asks: Who lives here, and who is speaking?
stories.text: The Himba of the Kunene, whose way of life is genuinely intact and should be visited carefully.
stories.title: The Himba

stories.asks: What is eaten here?
stories.text: Game meat over coals, biltong on every counter, and German bread that is actually German.
stories.title: Braai and Biltong

stories.asks: What is made here, and who makes it?
stories.text: Kavango wood carving, San ostrich-eggshell beadwork, and Herero doll making.
stories.title: Basketry and Ostrich Shell

stories.asks: What is kept, and who keeps it?
stories.text: Owambo, Herero, Damara, Nama, San and more, and German still on half the street signs.
stories.title: Eleven Peoples

stories.asks: What happened here, and what is left of it?
stories.text: A diamond town the desert has taken back, and the German colonial coast at Lüderitz.
stories.title: Kolmanskop and the Coast

stories.asks: What is it like to live here this decade?
stories.text: Windhoek on the highveld, and Swakopmund where German architecture meets Atlantic fog.
stories.title: Windhoek and Swakopmund

stories.arcTitle: What is wild, and what is being kept wild
stories.asks: What lives here, and who is protecting it?
stories.text: Elephant and rhino that walk sixty kilometres between water, and lion that hunt seals.
stories.title: Desert-Adapted Wildlife

stories.asks: What is the shape of this country?
stories.text: Fifty-five million years old, and dunes at Sossusvlei three hundred metres high.
stories.title: The Namib

stories.asks: What would you not have found on your own?
stories.text: The far north-west: Epupa, the Himba, and roads that need two vehicles.
stories.title: The Kunene

stories.arcTitle: The first thing you would see
stories.asks: What does this country open with?
stories.text: Afrobeats and Nollywood came from here, and it is worth seeing where.
stories.title: The Culture Everyone Else Is Watching

stories.asks: Who lives here, and who is speaking?

stories.title: Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, Fulani

stories.text: Suya off the grill at night, egusi with pounded yam, and the jollof question again.
stories.title: Jollof, Suya and Egusi

stories.text: Benin bronze casting still practised in Igun street, and adire resist-dyed cloth in Abeokuta.
stories.title: Bronze, Adire and Aso Oke

stories.asks: What is kept, and who keeps it?
stories.text: Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa and around five hundred more, in one country.
stories.title: Five Hundred Languages

stories.asks: What happened here, and what is left of it?
stories.text: The Benin bronzes are the reason half the museums of Europe have a Nigeria problem.
stories.title: The Bronzes

stories.asks: What is it like to live here this decade?
stories.text: Lagos on the lagoon, purpose-built Abuja in the middle, and Kano's thousand-year-old walls.
stories.title: Lagos, Abuja, Kano

stories.arcTitle: What is wild, and what is being kept wild

stories.title: Yankari and Gashaka

stories.title: Mangrove to Sahel

stories.text: Gorillas, canopy forest, Big Five and a lake shore, all within three hours of a capital you can walk at night.
stories.title: Small Country, Nothing Missing

stories.asks: Who lives here, and who is speaking?
stories.text: Cultural villages near Musanze where former poachers now guide, and the beekeepers and potters of the Virunga foothills.
stories.title: Living Memory

stories.asks: What is eaten here?
stories.text: Grilled goat brochettes, cassava leaf isombe, tilapia from Kivu, and some of the best coffee grown anywhere.
stories.title: Brochettes and Isombe

stories.asks: What is made here, and who makes it?
stories.text: Geometric imigongo panels in black, white and ochre, and the woven agaseke peace basket that is on the coat of arms.
stories.title: Imigongo and Agaseke

stories.asks: What is kept, and who keeps it?
stories.text: The Intore warriors' dance, the inanga zither, and drumming that was once the property of the king alone.
stories.title: Intore, the Dance of Heroes

stories.asks: What happened here, and what is left of it?
stories.text: The Kigali Genocide Memorial is where any honest visit to Rwanda starts, and it explains everything that came after.
stories.title: Memory and Reconstruction

stories.asks: What is it like to live here this decade?
stories.text: Built along ridge lines, swept every morning, and with a monthly Umuganda when the whole city cleans it together.
stories.title: Kigali, Across the Ridges

stories.arcTitle: What is wild, and what is being kept wild
stories.asks: What lives here, and who is protecting it?
stories.text: Ten habituated families on the Virunga slopes, one hour with them, eight people at a time.
stories.title: Face to Face with Gorillas

stories.asks: What is the shape of this country?
stories.text: Almost every hillside in Rwanda is farmed in contour terraces — the landscape is entirely made by hand.
stories.title: Terraces to the Horizon

stories.asks: What would you not have found on your own?
stories.text: Rwanda's newest national park, a recovering forest between Nyungwe and the volcanoes that almost nobody visits.
stories.title: Gishwati-Mukura

stories.arcTitle: The first thing you would see
stories.asks: What does this country open with?
stories.text: Stable, straightforward, six hours from Europe, and the friendliest reputation on the coast.
stories.title: The Easy Door to West Africa

stories.asks: Who lives here, and who is speaking?
stories.text: Wolof across the country, Serer in the delta, and the Diola of Casamance.
stories.title: Wolof, Serer and Diola

stories.asks: What is eaten here?
stories.text: Rice and fish, cooked in one pot, and the national dish by common consent.
stories.title: Thieboudienne

stories.asks: What is made here, and who makes it?
stories.text: Sous-verre glass painting, and the strip-woven cloth of the Manjak weavers.
stories.title: Glass Painting and Weaving

stories.asks: What is kept, and who keeps it?
stories.text: The word means hospitality, and it is the thing the country most wants you to notice.
stories.title: Teranga

stories.asks: What happened here, and what is left of it?
stories.text: The old colonial capital on its island in the river mouth, with the Faidherbe bridge.
stories.title: Saint-Louis

stories.asks: What is it like to live here this decade?
stories.text: The most westerly city in Africa, on a peninsula, with the ocean on three sides.
stories.title: Dakar

stories.arcTitle: What is wild, and what is being kept wild
stories.asks: What lives here, and who is protecting it?
stories.text: Three million migrating birds winter in the Djoudj — one of the great bird sites on earth.
stories.title: Djoudj

stories.asks: What is the shape of this country?
stories.text: The Sine-Saloum mangrove delta, the Casamance forest, and Sahel sand in the north.
stories.title: Delta and Dune

stories.asks: What would you not have found on your own?
stories.text: The Bassari and Bedik villages of the south-east, up in the hills, and rarely visited.
stories.title: Bassari Country

stories.arcTitle: The first thing you would see
stories.asks: What does this country open with?
stories.text: Granite in mid-ocean, a palm that grows nowhere else, and tortoises older than the state.
stories.title: Nowhere Else Is Built Like This

stories.asks: Who lives here, and who is speaking?
stories.text: A hundred thousand people across a hundred and fifteen islands, most on three of them.
stories.title: Island Life

stories.asks: What is eaten here?
stories.text: Grilled fish, coconut curry, breadfruit, and a chilli sauce that is not a suggestion.
stories.title: Fish, Coconut and Chilli

stories.asks: What is made here, and who makes it?
stories.text: Pirogue building on La Digue, and coconut palm weaving still done by hand.
stories.title: Boatbuilding and Weaving

stories.asks: What is kept, and who keeps it?
stories.text: African, French, Indian and Chinese, in one Creole language and one kitchen.
stories.title: Creole

stories.asks: What happened here, and what is left of it?
stories.text: A thousand kilometres out, with a hundred thousand giant tortoises and almost no people.
stories.title: Aldabra

stories.asks: What is it like to live here this decade?
stories.text: One of the smallest capitals in the world, with a clock tower and a market.
stories.title: Victoria

stories.arcTitle: What is wild, and what is being kept wild
stories.asks: What lives here, and who is protecting it?
stories.text: The black parrot, the magpie robin, and giant tortoises that live free on Curieuse.
stories.title: Endemic Everywhere

stories.asks: What is the shape of this country?
stories.text: Granite in the inner islands, coral atolls in the outer, and a thousand kilometres between.
stories.title: Forty-Three Granite Islands

stories.asks: What would you not have found on your own?
stories.text: No real roads and few cars — an island best measured in bicycle hours.
stories.title: La Digue by Bicycle

stories.arcTitle: The first thing you would see
stories.asks: What does this country open with?
stories.text: Mountain, desert, reef, bush and two of Africa's most interesting cities, on roads you can drive yourself.
stories.title: Two Weeks, Four Countries' Worth

stories.asks: Who lives here, and who is speaking?
stories.text: Ndebele wall painting, Zulu beadwork with its own grammar, and Xhosa initiation still practised in the Eastern Cape.
stories.title: Zulu, Xhosa, Ndebele

stories.asks: What is eaten here?
stories.text: Fire is a national institution; Durban curry and Cape Malay bobotie came from two very different arrivals.
stories.title: Braai, Bunny Chow, Curry

stories.asks: What is made here, and who makes it?
stories.text: Beadwork, wire sculpture and telephone-wire baskets, sold everywhere and made properly in very few places.
stories.title: Ndebele Beadwork

stories.asks: What is kept, and who keeps it?
stories.text: Zulu, Xhosa, Afrikaans and eight more, plus the Cape Malay cooking that came with the slave trade.
stories.title: Eleven Languages

stories.asks: What happened here, and what is left of it?
stories.text: The Sterkfontein caves have produced more early hominin fossils than any other site on the planet.
stories.title: The Cradle of Humankind

stories.asks: What is it like to live here this decade?
stories.text: One built around a mountain and a harbour, the other on a gold reef, and nothing about them is alike.
stories.title: Cape Town and Johannesburg

stories.arcTitle: What is wild, and what is being kept wild
stories.asks: What lives here, and who is protecting it?
stories.text: Kruger and the private Sabi Sands reserves beside it, where the leopards have been watched for generations.
stories.title: The Big Five, Close

stories.asks: What is the shape of this country?
stories.text: The Cape Floral Kingdom is the smallest and richest of the six on earth, and most of it grows nowhere else.
stories.title: Fynbos and the Garden Route

stories.asks: What would you not have found on your own?
stories.text: Hole in the Wall and the Transkei green hills, and the Karoo's enormous silence in the other direction.
stories.title: The Wild Coast and Karoo

stories.arcTitle: The first thing you would see
stories.asks: What does this country open with?
stories.text: Summit Africa's highest mountain, cross the Serengeti and sleep on the Indian Ocean, in the same fortnight.
stories.title: Mountain, Plain and Reef

stories.asks: Who lives here, and who is speaking?
stories.text: One of the last hunter-gatherer peoples in Africa, speaking a click language unrelated to anything nearby.
stories.title: The Hadzabe of Lake Eyasi

stories.asks: What is eaten here?
stories.text: Cloves and cardamom from the Zanzibar plantations, grilled seafood at Forodhani, and ugali everywhere else.
stories.title: Spice, Ugali, Urojo

stories.asks: What is made here, and who makes it?
stories.text: Enamel-bright Tingatinga painting from Dar es Salaam, and Makonde ebony carving from the southern plateau.
stories.title: Tingatinga and Makonde

stories.asks: What is kept, and who keeps it?
stories.text: Cattle-keepers on the northern plains, coffee farmers on the mountain, and a coast that has always faced east.
stories.title: Maasai, Chagga, Swahili

stories.asks: What happened here, and what is left of it?
stories.text: Olduvai Gorge holds the earliest human record; the coast holds a thousand years of Indian Ocean trade.
stories.title: Olduvai and the Coast

stories.asks: What is it like to live here this decade?
stories.text: Harbour of peace: the ferry terminal, the fish market at Kivukoni, and the dhows still working the channel.
stories.title: Dar es Salaam

stories.arcTitle: What is wild, and what is being kept wild
stories.asks: What lives here, and who is protecting it?
stories.text: Lion, leopard, elephant, buffalo and rhino, plus the largest elephant herds left in East Africa.
stories.title: The Big Five, and Then Some

stories.asks: What is the shape of this country?
stories.text: A collapsed caldera twenty kilometres across with its own permanent population of thirty thousand animals.
stories.title: The Ngorongoro Crater

stories.asks: What would you not have found on your own?
stories.text: The south and west: huge elephant populations, hippo crowded into shrinking pools, and no other vehicles.
stories.title: Ruaha and Katavi

stories.arcTitle: The first thing you would see
stories.asks: What does this country open with?
stories.text: An amphitheatre on Monday and a dune camp on Thursday, in a country the size of England.
stories.title: Rome, and the Sahara, in One Week

stories.asks: Who lives here, and who is speaking?
stories.text: The ksour of Tataouine, and the underground houses of Matmata.
stories.title: The Berber South

stories.asks: What is eaten here?
stories.text: Friday couscous, brik straight out of the pan, and harissa on everything.
stories.title: Couscous, Brik and Harissa

stories.asks: What is made here, and who makes it?
stories.text: Roman mosaic technique still taught, Nabeul ceramic, and Berber silver from the south.
stories.title: Mosaic, Ceramic and Silver

stories.asks: What is kept, and who keeps it?
stories.text: Four layers, all of them still visible, and often in the same town.
stories.title: Punic, Roman, Arab, Berber

stories.asks: What happened here, and what is left of it?
stories.text: Tunis, Sousse and Kairouan — Kairouan's mosque is among the oldest in the Maghreb.
stories.title: The Medinas

stories.asks: What is it like to live here this decade?
stories.text: Tunis at the head of its lake, and Sfax's walled medina working as a medina still.
stories.title: Tunis and Sfax

stories.arcTitle: What is wild, and what is being kept wild
stories.asks: What lives here, and who is protecting it?
stories.text: Ichkeul's wintering waterfowl, and the desert fox and gazelle of the south.
stories.title: Ichkeul and the Desert

stories.asks: What is the shape of this country?
stories.text: The Cap Bon coast, the olive Sahel, and the salt flats of the Chott el Djerid.
stories.title: Coast to Chott

stories.asks: What would you not have found on your own?
stories.text: Vaulted grain stores stacked four storeys high, and almost nobody there.
stories.title: Ksar Ouled Soltane

stories.arcTitle: The first thing you would see
stories.asks: What does this country open with?
stories.text: Nowhere else puts gorillas, chimpanzees, the Big Five, a snowline and the Nile within one week of driving.
stories.title: Half the World's Gorillas

stories.asks: Who lives here, and who is speaking?
stories.text: The Batwa, forest people of the southwest, and the Karamojong cattle-keepers of the northeast plains.
stories.title: Batwa and Karamojong

stories.asks: What is eaten here?
stories.text: Steamed green banana with groundnut sauce, chicken cooked in banana leaf, and an egg rolled in a chapati on every corner.
stories.title: Rolex, Matoke, Luwombo

stories.asks: What is made here, and who makes it?
stories.text: Bark cloth from the mutuba fig, made in Buganda for six hundred years and now UNESCO-listed.
stories.title: Bark Cloth and Basketry

stories.asks: What is kept, and who keeps it?
stories.text: Uganda's kingdoms were never abolished for long — Buganda, Bunyoro and Toro still hold court.
stories.title: The Kingdom of Buganda

stories.asks: What happened here, and what is left of it?
stories.text: Royal drums, regalia and clan structures that survived the protectorate, the 1966 crisis and the 1970s.
stories.title: Kingdoms Still Standing

stories.asks: What is it like to live here this decade?
stories.text: A capital built across hills and traffic, with the Gaddafi Mosque minaret giving the best view of all of it.
stories.title: Kampala on Seven Hills

stories.arcTitle: What is wild, and what is being kept wild
stories.asks: What lives here, and who is protecting it?
stories.text: Mountain gorillas in Bwindi, chimpanzees in Kibale, and tree-climbing lions in the Ishasha sector.
stories.title: Wildlife Encounters

stories.asks: What is the shape of this country?
stories.text: Crater lakes around Fort Portal, papyrus swamp on the Nile, and the Rwenzori snowline sitting on the equator.
stories.title: Green, End to End

stories.asks: What would you not have found on your own?
stories.text: The furthest park from Kampala and the emptiest: Narus valley, the Morungole range, and cheetah nobody photographs.
stories.title: Kidepo Valley

stories.arcTitle: The first thing you would see
stories.asks: What does this country open with?
stories.text: Zambia kept the walking safari, the small camp and the empty park while its neighbours scaled up.
stories.title: Wilderness, Still Unmanaged

stories.asks: Who lives here, and who is speaking?
stories.text: The Lozi live with the flood — moving cattle, homes and the king himself when the Zambezi rises.
stories.title: The Barotse Floodplain

stories.asks: What is eaten here?
stories.text: Maize nshima with relish, dried kapenta from the lakes, and fresh bream out of the Zambezi.
stories.title: Nshima and Kapenta

stories.asks: What is made here, and who makes it?
stories.text: Tight coiled baskets from the Western Province, and copper worked on the belt that built the economy.
stories.title: Basketry and Copper

stories.asks: What is kept, and who keeps it?
stories.text: Seventy-three ethnic groups, seven official languages, and a royal barge ceremony older than the country.
stories.title: Lozi, Bemba, Tonga

stories.asks: What happened here, and what is left of it?
stories.text: World Heritage since 1989, shared with Zimbabwe, and named by the Kololo long before anyone renamed it.
stories.title: Mosi-oa-Tunya, UNESCO

stories.asks: What is it like to live here this decade?
stories.text: The centre of everything: Kabwata market, the Great East Road, and the flights that get you to the parks.
stories.title: Lusaka

stories.arcTitle: What is wild, and what is being kept wild
stories.asks: What lives here, and who is protecting it?
stories.text: The South Luangwa has one of the densest leopard populations in Africa, and the best chance of seeing one hunting.
stories.title: Leopard Country

stories.asks: What is the shape of this country?
stories.text: Escarpment, floodplain and winterthorn forest, with the river braiding through the middle of all of it.
stories.title: The Zambezi Valley

stories.asks: What would you not have found on your own?
stories.text: The second largest wildebeest migration in Africa, on a plain almost nobody has heard of, reachable only in the dry.
stories.title: Liuwa Plain

stories.arcTitle: The first thing you would see
stories.asks: What does this country open with?
stories.text: The hardest guiding exam in Africa, and a stone city most visitors have never heard of.
stories.title: Guides, and Great Ruins

stories.asks: Who lives here, and who is speaking?
stories.text: Zimbabwean stone sculpture is the country's clearest contemporary export.
stories.title: The Stone Sculptors

stories.asks: What is eaten here?
stories.text: Sadza with relish, and meat over coals wherever there is a fire and company.
stories.title: Sadza and Braai

stories.asks: What is made here, and who makes it?
stories.text: Serpentine carving, Binga basketry, and wire sculpture sold on every roadside.
stories.title: Stone, Basket and Wire

stories.asks: What is kept, and who keeps it?
stories.text: Shona across the centre and east, Ndebele in the west, and stone sculpture from both.
stories.title: Shona and Ndebele

stories.asks: What happened here, and what is left of it?
stories.text: Khami's terraces, and the Matobo hills where Mzilikazi and Rhodes are both buried.
stories.title: Khami and Matobo

stories.asks: What is it like to live here this decade?
stories.text: Harare on the highveld, and Bulawayo's wide colonial grid built for turning an ox wagon.
stories.title: Harare and Bulawayo

stories.arcTitle: What is wild, and what is being kept wild
stories.asks: What lives here, and who is protecting it?
stories.text: Forty thousand elephant in Hwange, drinking at pumped pans through the dry season.
stories.title: Hwange's Elephant

stories.asks: What is the shape of this country?
stories.text: Granite kopjes across the highveld, and the Zambezi escarpment dropping into the valley.
stories.title: Highveld and Escarpment

stories.asks: What would you not have found on your own?
stories.text: A mountain range on the Mozambique border that you walk into and camp in.
stories.title: Chimanimani
